source: Zhou et al. (2026) Externalization in LLM Agents: A Unified Review of Memory, Skills, Protocols and Harness Engineering
finding: Review argues agent progress comes from moving cognitive burdens out of the model into memory, skills, protocols and a harness. It uses Norman's cognitive artifact idea (representational transformation) as the frame.
numbers: No new experiment. Claims: memory externalizes state across time, skills externalize procedure, protocols externalize interaction structure. Cites Norman 1991/1993 and Kirsh, not new Hutchins data.
quote: Cognitive artifacts do not change human capabilities. They change the task.
limits: Conceptual review. It is an interpretation of existing work, not a test of distributed cognition predictions. Authors choose which results count.
agent_relevance: Supports our design view: the schema is an external artifact. Recall to recognition, improvised to composed, ad hoc to contract is a usable checklist for what to externalize.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Externalization in LLM Agents: A Unified Review of Memory, Skills, Protocols and Harness Engineering
finding: Review claims many of the largest reliability gains in practice come from changing the environment around the model, not the weights. Weights, context, harness are its three layers.
numbers: Qualitative: no pooled effect size in the opened introduction. Thesis is stated across the review.
limits: Reasoning is by citation, so the claim is only as strong as the cited ablations. Selection bias possible.
agent_relevance: Fits our plan (scaffold, not training). Treat as framing, and back each element with a measured ablation like c19 and c20.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: 25 LLM agents with a memory stream, reflection and planning. Removing each component lowered rated believability, so the external memory and plan structure carried the behaviour.
numbers: Ablation, 100 human raters ranking 5 conditions, TrueSkill mu: full 29.89, no reflection 26.88, no reflection or planning 25.64, human crowdworkers 22.95, no memory/planning/reflection 21.21 (sigma about 0.7). Full vs fully ablated d=8.16. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(4)=150.29, p<0.001.
limits: Rating is of believability, not task success. Crowdworker baseline wrote role-play answers. Single model (ChatGPT). Agents hallucinated embellishments.
agent_relevance: Shows a memory and reflection artifact outside the model drives measurable quality. Evidence for external state, but on a social-simulation measure.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents
finding: Information spread between agents with no user prompting, a transactive-memory-like effect with conversation as the only channel.
numbers: Sam's mayoral candidacy known to 1 agent (4%), then 8 (32%). Isabella's party known to 1 (4%), then 13 (52%), over two game days, 25 agents.
limits: Single run per measure as reported. Hallucinated embellishment was checked by memory-stream audit, and some did occur. Not a task benchmark.
agent_relevance: Shared conversation spreads facts but also errors. Any shared notes between agents need a source check (G2/G3).

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several model copies propose, read each other and revise. Debate beat single answer, reflection and majority vote on math and chess in this paper.
numbers: 3 agents, 2 rounds, ChatGPT. Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9.
quote: Despite answers being incorrect, language models would confidently affirm that their answer is correct
limits: Same model for all agents. Authors say debates converged but not always to the right answer, and models stayed confident. Costlier. Later work (c07, c08) does not reproduce the edge.
agent_relevance: The original positive case for socially distributed reasoning in LLMs. It conflicts with our G4: copies of one model are not independent. Treat as a hint only.

source: Du et al. (2023) Multiagent Debate
finding: Debate also raised factual accuracy and reduced hallucination in biographies and MMLU.
numbers: Biographies: single 66.0, reflection 68.3, debate 73.8. MMLU: 63.9, 57.7, 71.1. Chess move validity: 29.3, 38.8, 45.2.
limits: Reflection lowered MMLU from 63.9 to 57.7, so self-critique alone hurt there. On facts the model was sure of, agents would not change their answer.
agent_relevance: Matches G1/G2: self-critique without an outside signal can hurt. Debate's gain comes from other copies, not from doubt.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
finding: Benchmark of debate protocols against self-consistency and other prompts: debate does not reliably win in default form. Tuning how strongly agents agree at the start moved Multi-Persona from worst to best.
numbers: Multiple-choice benchmarks incl. MedQA and USMLE. Multi-Persona (devil agent) lowered performance versus relying on the first agent alone. Agreement-intensity prompt raised accuracy and beat Medprompt and self-consistency after tuning. A MedQA configuration reaches 61%.
limits: Gains depend on a prompt hyperparameter tuned on the benchmark. Medical multiple-choice mostly. Tuned result may not transfer.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G4 in the negative: forced disagreement hurt. Agreement level is a control knob worth keeping in code.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Large re-test of 5 debate methods: they usually do not beat chain of thought or self-consistency even with much more compute.
numbers: 5 methods x 9 benchmarks x 4 models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-8b, Llama3.1-70b, Claude-3.5-haiku), 3 repeats. Over 36 configs by ANOVA, SoM, EoT, ChatEval and AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of cases at best. SoM lost to CoT on all 9 sets with GPT-4o-mini. Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU: only AgentVerse won (+0.85%), others lost by 3.60% or more.
limits: Compares to CoT and SC in single-model settings. Does not test tuned or trained debate.
agent_relevance: This is the failed-replication evidence for homogeneous multi-agent debate. Our single agent should not copy a multi-voice debate.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Mixing different models (heterogeneity) consistently helped debate. It was the one fix that worked.
numbers: Heter-SoM +6.4% over SoM-average of the two models alone. Heter-EoT +8.2% over EoT-average. All heterogeneous MAD beat CoT-average by up to 5.8%.
limits: Two-model mixes only; authors do not optimize the design. Gains smaller on ChatEval and AgentVerse.
agent_relevance: Matches our gap brief: errors correlate within one model. Distribution helps only when the nodes differ. With one model, distribute over tools and code instead.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Annotated 1600+ traces from 7 multi-agent frameworks and built a 14-mode failure taxonomy. Failures are mostly design and coordination faults.
numbers: Failure rate 41% to 86.7% across 7 open-source systems. Taxonomy from 150 traces, kappa 0.88. LLM-judge annotator kappa 0.77. Share of failures: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%.
limits: Frameworks are open-source ones of 2024-25. Taxonomy built by the authors; the scalable annotator is itself an LLM.
agent_relevance: A list of how a distributed LLM system breaks. Over three quarters are structure or communication faults, so a fixed program-controlled flow with checks avoids many.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Weak verification is a main failure. Adding a high-level task-objective verification step to ChatDev improved success.
numbers: +15.6% task success on ProgramDev from the added verification step (Appendix H intervention).
limits: One framework and one benchmark. Existing verifiers often only checked that code compiled.
agent_relevance: Supports G3: verification must check the real objective, not surface properties.

source: Hong et al. (2023) MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
finding: Encodes human team standard operating procedures (roles, structured documents passed between roles) into prompts. A division of labour with artifacts as the channel.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1 85.9%, MBPP 87.7%. SoftwareDev (70 tasks) executability 3.75 vs ChatDev 2.25 (scale 1-4). Human revision cost 0.83 vs 2.5 (table layout garbled in extraction, values read by position). Executable feedback loop added.
limits: Small SoftwareDev set built by authors. Compared with older baselines. Roles not shown to beat a single strong agent with the same structure.
agent_relevance: The gain is plausibly from structured documents and executable feedback (artifacts), not persona. Fits G2: revise from real output.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
finding: Layered mix of different LLMs, each reading the previous layer's outputs, beat GPT-4o on chat benchmarks using only open models.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 length-controlled: MoA 65.1% (+/-0.6), MoA with GPT-4o 65.7%, MoA-Lite 59.3%, GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-4o 57.5%.
limits: Win rate judged by an LLM, open to verbosity and self-preference bias (our G5). Many calls per answer. Not verifiable tasks.
agent_relevance: Again heterogeneity is the lever. A judge-based score is weak evidence for our correctness-based loop.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Scaling Teams or Scaling Time? (LLMA-Mem)
finding: Memory design for multi-agent teams that includes a transactive memory of who is good at what. Role-local memory beat shared memory.
numbers: MultiAgentBench, 4 models. Ablation (coding, Qwen3-32B): local topology best, shared and hybrid worse. Consolidation interval 5 best; 2, 10, 20 worse. AAS gains vs no-memory +0.27 to +5.92. Token cost 9.4% to 71.7% below MARBLE and A-Mem.
limits: Gains vs no-memory are small in several cells (e.g. +0.27). One exception lost AAS (Qwen3-Next-80B research). Preprint.
agent_relevance: More sharing is not better: role-specific stores avoided cross-role interference. Argues for narrow, scoped notes in our schema.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Scaling Teams or Scaling Time? (LLMA-Mem)
finding: Larger teams do not always do better; smaller teams with good memory can beat larger ones. Memory lowers cost by compacting episodes into procedures.
numbers: Non-monotonic scaling in team size. On DeepSeek-v3.2 baseline memories drifted negative at the end of long runs while LLMA-Mem stayed positive (CMA ends 167.0 coding, 321.8 research).
limits: Coordination score fell in some cells even when task score rose.
agent_relevance: Supports one agent with good external memory over many agents.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM)
finding: Population-level store of agent trajectories that other agents retrieve (Wegner's transactive memory at agent scale). Retrieval raised success and cut steps.
numbers: ALFWorld success 47.08% to 55.11% (+8.0 points), steps 11.77 to 11.18. WebArena 18.18% to 20% (+2 points), steps 22.0 to 20.3. Tokens per successful episode down 11 to 34%. Reranker reaches 64.3% on ALFWorld (+17.2 over no retrieval).
limits: Small gain on WebArena. Index-size curve non-monotonic (dip at 50% on WebArena). Version 2 dated Oct 2026.
agent_relevance: A shared trajectory library is a real artifact that helps. A single agent can keep its own library of solved cases the same way.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM)
finding: Agents decide per step whether to retrieve, because indiscriminate retrieval dilutes context. Many contributors mattered more than a few.
numbers: A RetrievalPlanner gates retrieval each step. Top-20 candidates, one reranked unit passed to the agent. Small producer groups supplied 31.8% of retrieved ALFWorld trajectories. Same-type-only retrieval gave 59.9%, still above the 47.1% baseline but below the full pool.
limits: Mechanism is partly correlational. Single benchmark pair.
agent_relevance: Retrieval should be signal-triggered (G1 style), with a budget of one item.

source: Zhang et al. (2025/2026) CoThinker: Cognitive Load Theory for multi-agent LLM design
finding: Multi-agent setup that splits intrinsic load across specialists and shares a collective working memory. Gains appear on reasoning-heavy tasks and vanish on simple instruction following.
numbers: Table 15, GPT-5-Nano CoThinker: Zebra Puzzle 75.75, Spatial 88.00, Math Comp 89.13. Paper reports significant gains over CoT and other baselines on some task groups and a pooled loss of 3.8% on instruction following (p<0.001).
limits: Percent columns were hard to read from the extracted tables, so only the stated boundary is firm. Lab-built tasks plus a fabricated high-load set. Authors' own framework.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: distribution costs coordination overhead, so use it only on high-load problems. Our router should not split easy items.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Changing only the interface between model and computer, with fewer, simpler commands and tight feedback, raised resolve rate. A clean cognitive artifact test.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite (300): SWE-agent 18.0% vs Shell-only 7.3% (+10.7 points, 64% relative per paper wording). Full SWE-bench 12.47% (286/2294). HumanEvalFix pass@1 87.7%. Claude 3 Opus 10.5%.
limits: GPT-4 Turbo era numbers; frontier models now score far higher. ACI was designed on GPT-4 Turbo and tuned on Lite. Ablations noisy (std about 3 to 7 points).
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence here that the artifact, not the model, moves results. Design for the model: small action set, guardrails, concise feedback.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent
finding: Specific interface pieces mattered: a linter guardrail on edits, file viewer size, history handling.
numbers: Without linting 15.0% vs 18.0% (-3.0). No file-editor interface 10.3% (+/-7.7). Viewer of 30 lines 14.3%, full file 12.7%, 100 lines 18.0%. Last-5-observations history 18.0%, full history 15.0%.
limits: Differences of 2 to 3 points are inside the reported error bars. Single model.
agent_relevance: Guardrails that block bad edits help error recovery (our G2). Too little or too much context both hurt, so cap what the model sees each step.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt
finding: Human side of offloading to an LLM: essay writers using an LLM showed weaker brain connectivity and poorer recall of their own text than search or no-tool writers.
numbers: 54 participants in 3 sessions (LLM, search engine, brain-only), 18 in session 4 crossover, with EEG. In session 1, 83.3% (15/18) of the LLM group could not give a correct quote vs 11.1% (2/18) in each of the search and brain-only groups. Lower ownership in the LLM group.
limits: Small sample, essay task, preprint, EEG interpretation debated. Session 4 only 18 people. Not a test of team performance.
agent_relevance: Warns that an external helper can cut the human's own encoding. Keep human checkpoints as active steps, not passive reads.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (CHI)
finding: Survey of knowledge workers: more confidence in the AI went with less critical thinking effort; more self-confidence went with more.
numbers: 319 knowledge workers, 936 first-hand examples. Task-specific self-confidence and confidence in GenAI both predict whether critical thinking was enacted and its effort. Work shifts to verification, integration and task stewardship.
limits: Self-report only, correlational, convenience sample, workers describing their own effort.
agent_relevance: Human-AI joint system risk: trust lowers checking. Our scaffold should force verification by code rather than ask human or model to remember.

source: Rosenbacke et al. (2026) From Consumption to Reflection (Relational Reflective Intelligence)
finding: Proposes an inference-time layer adding short reflection checkpoints around the human-LLM pair and calls the pair a joint reasoning system.
numbers: No measured results found in the opened text. Components: Rose-Frame, Architect's Pen, RRI workflow.
limits: Conceptual proposal, untested. Claims about relational drift are not shown with data.
agent_relevance: Low weight. Only supports the framing that errors compound between human and model; no effect size to use.

source: Wikipedia: Blackboard system (Hearsay-II lineage)
finding: Older AI built on shared-workspace cognition: independent knowledge sources write partial solutions to a common blackboard and a control shell schedules them. Hearsay-II (Erman et al. 1980) is the standard early case.
numbers: The page gives no accuracy or vocabulary numbers for Hearsay-II; only the 1980 citation.
limits: Secondary source and thin. Hearsay-II figures must come from the 1980 paper.
agent_relevance: Ancestor of shared-notes designs. Our S-states and operators act like knowledge sources; the program is the control shell.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) MAST, cross-read with Zhang et al. (2025)
finding: Cross-read: the MAST authors say multi-agent gains are often minimal against single-agent frameworks or best-of-N, which matches the re-tests in c08.
numbers: MAST intro: gains 'often minimal' against single agent or best-of-N. Zhang et al.: debate wins in about 15% of 36 configs.
limits: MAST intro claim cites other work; not independently re-run here.
agent_relevance: Pattern across independent groups: homogeneous multi-agent gives little over cheap baselines.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Externalization in LLM Agents: A Unified Review of Memory, Skills, Protocols and Harness Engineering
finding: The review treats LLM agents as themselves artifacts inside human externalization. It does not cite measured tests of Hutchins's claim that cognition is a property of the whole system.
numbers: No Hutchins empirical numbers. Searches found no LLM paper that directly tests Hutchins's system-level predictions (propagation of representational state).
limits: Absence found with limited search (APIs rate-limited, 2 of 6 web searches used for this), so a missing study is possible.
agent_relevance: Gap: the concept is used as a design metaphor, not tested. Say so, and test the pieces ourselves.

source: Synthesis across Park 2023, Hong 2023, Yang 2024, Kim 2026
finding: Methods from this subfield already inside LLM agent loops: external memory stream with retrieval (c03), role-split artifacts (c12), a curated action interface (c19), shared trajectory index (c16).
limits: Each was built for its own task; none isolates one distributed-cognition principle.
agent_relevance: Menu for the schema: persistent memory, interface design and scoped retrieval have measured gains. Multi-voice debate with one model does not.
